lessons.title: Who Writes the Cheques in India: Angels, Angel Networks, Micro VCs, VCs and Government Schemes

children.text: You run a two-person startup in Indore, you need ₹1.5 crore, and you have decided the money is worth the dilution. Now comes the practical question nobody answers in the funding headlines: who do you actually call? India has a crowded and confusing supply side, from a doctor in Nagpur writing ₹5 lakh cheques to a ₹5,000 crore fund in Bengaluru, with government schemes, accelerators and syndicates in between. Each has a different cheque size, a different decision speed and a different price. Approach the wrong one and you waste three months.

body.text: Match the cheque to the source. Every investor type has a size band they cannot go below or above, because of how their own money is structured. Pitching a ₹1 crore round to a fund that must deploy ₹40 crore per deal is not ambition, it is a wasted quarter.

children.text: Individual Angels

markDefs.definition: An individual who invests personal money into early-stage startups, usually in exchange for equity or a convertible instrument.

children.text: An
angel investor

spends their own savings, answers to nobody and can decide over one coffee. In India the active pool is largely founders and senior operators: people like Kunal Shah of CRED, Rajan Anandan and the Snapdeal founders through Titan Capital have all backed early companies. Below that famous layer sits a much larger group nobody writes about, including doctors, chartered accountants, family business owners and senior corporate executives who each write ₹5 lakh to ₹25 lakh cheques.

columns.label: The operator angel
points: Has built or scaled a company themselves
Brings introductions, hiring help and pattern recognition
Decides quickly because they understand the space
Expects to be called when things go wrong
Their name on your cap table helps the next round

columns.label: The wealth angel
points: Has capital from a profession, business or inheritance
Brings money, and sometimes local business networks
May take longer and ask for more comfort
Often needs education on why startups fail
Manage expectations early or handle unhappy calls later

body.label: Where first cheques actually come from
body.context: Angels and funds see far more deals than they can fund, so they filter by trust. An introduction from a founder they have already backed is worth more than the best cold email you will ever write.

children.text: Angel Networks, Syndicates and Platforms

One angel rarely fills a round. Networks and platforms solve that by pooling many small cheques behind one decision maker. Indian Angel Network, Mumbai Angels, Venture Catalysts, LetsVenture and AngelList India all do versions of this. The mechanics matter to you as a founder:
A lead does the work.
One investor diligences the company, sets the terms and commits first. Everyone else follows that lead.
Many names, one line on the cap table.
Most platforms pool investors into a single vehicle, so you deal with one entity instead of thirty individuals. That keeps future rounds simple.
The lead is paid in carry.
Syndicate leads typically keep a share of the profits from the investors who follow them, so their incentive is a real exit, not just a closed round.

An individual writing a personal cheque needs no registration. Pooled angel vehicles are different: they are regulated by SEBI as angel funds, a sub-category of Category I Alternative Investment Funds under the SEBI (Alternative Investment Funds) Regulations, 2012.
Who can join:
individual angel investors have to meet a net tangible asset test, excluding the value of their main home, or qualify as accredited investors.
Cheque limits per startup:
an angel fund's investment in any single company sits inside a prescribed minimum and maximum band.
Why it matters to you:

a SEBI-registered vehicle brings documentation, reporting and a clean paper trail that later investors and auditors will check. Money pooled informally from many small investors without a registered vehicle can create real problems at your next round.

SEBI has amended these thresholds more than once, including changes aimed at accredited investors, so check the current regulations or ask your company secretary rather than relying on numbers quoted in a pitch deck.
Accelerators and Incubators

These sell a package: a small cheque, a fixed programme, mentors and a demo day in front of investors, usually for about 5% to 10% of the company. Antler India and 100X.VC run India-focused cohorts, Y Combinator has backed many Indian founders from abroad, and campus incubators at the IITs and IIMs, along with state bodies like T-Hub in Hyderabad and Kerala Startup Mission, offer space, grants and mentoring, often on far softer terms.

body.text: Judge an accelerator by the fundraising outcomes of the cohort two batches ahead of you, not by the brochure. Ask those founders directly whether the introductions converted into term sheets. If the equity cost is 7% and the network does not reliably produce a next round, you have sold a big piece of your company for a certificate.

children.text: Micro VCs and Institutional VC Funds

markDefs.definition: The investors who supply money to a fund, such as family offices, insurers, pension funds and government fund-of-funds. They do not pick the individual investments.

children.text: Both invest other people's money, raised from
limited partners

, and both are usually registered with SEBI as Alternative Investment Funds. The difference is arithmetic. A ₹200 crore micro VC can write ₹2 crore cheques and still build a portfolio of 40 companies. A ₹4,000 crore fund cannot, because 40 companies would mean ₹100 crore each. Fund size therefore dictates stage, cheque size and how much ownership they must take.

stats.label: Corporate and strategic

stats.label: The structural rule
stats.context: A fund must own enough of a winner to move its own returns

body.title: Why a big fund cannot write a small cheque
body.prompt: A ₹3,000 crore VC fund plans to back 30 companies over its life, keeping half the corpus in reserve for follow-on rounds. What is the average size of its first cheque, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: Half of ₹3,000 crore is ₹1,500 crore for first cheques, spread across 30 companies: ₹1,500 ÷ 30 = ₹50 crore each. A fund built this way cannot write you a ₹2 crore cheque, however much the partner likes your idea. That is not rejection, it is arithmetic, and it is why you should target funds whose size matches your round.

children.text: Government Money

India runs one of the world's larger public startup support programmes, and most founders ignore it because the money is slow and unglamorous. It is also the only money on this page that does not take a board seat. The gateway to almost all of it is DPIIT recognition under Startup India, which is a free online registration for eligible companies.

cells: Grants for proof of concept and prototype development, plus larger amounts for market entry and commercialisation
Through approved incubators, as a grant or via convertible debentures or debt-linked instruments
Capital for SEBI-registered AIFs, operated by SIDBI
Indirectly: the AIFs invest in startups, so you never apply to it yourself
A guarantee that lets lenders offer loans without conventional collateral
Through banks, NBFCs and AIFs lending to DPIIT-recognised startups
Grants, subsidised space, patent cost support and matching capital
Directly, through bodies such as T-Hub, Kerala Startup Mission and state startup policies

body.label: Startup India: DPIIT recognition and schemes
body.description: The official portal for DPIIT startup recognition, the Startup India Seed Fund Scheme, the credit guarantee scheme and state policy listings. Check eligibility and current scheme terms here rather than relying on second-hand summaries.

body.text: Two cautions on public money. First, it is milestone linked and slow, so never build your runway plan around a grant that has not landed. Second, treat anyone who offers to "arrange funding" for an upfront fee or a percentage as a red flag. Legitimate investors, incubators and government schemes do not charge founders a success fee to receive capital.

body.title: Who should this founder call?
body.question: A Coimbatore hardware startup has a working prototype of an industrial sensor, two pilot customers and no revenue. The founders need ₹1.5 crore for tooling and certification. Which source is the most realistic first stop?
options: A ₹4,000 crore institutional VC fund that led three Series B rounds this year
A mix of angels and a micro VC, alongside an incubator or state grant for the certification work
A private equity fund that buys profitable manufacturers
A bank term loan secured against the founders' homes
body.explanation: ₹1.5 crore at prototype stage is angel, micro VC and grant territory, and hardware certification costs are exactly what incubator and state schemes fund. The large VC cannot deploy such a small cheque, PE funds buy mature profitable businesses, and betting the family home on an unproven product is the kind of risk equity exists to avoid.

body.title: Two offers, one seat on the cap table
body.scenario:
Meher runs a Jaipur B2B marketplace for block-printed textiles with ₹80 lakh of annual revenue. She has two offers for the same ₹1 crore.
Offer A: an accelerator programme, ₹1 crore for 8% of the company, a three-month cohort in Bengaluru and a demo day.
Offer B: a syndicate on an angel platform, ₹1 crore for 12%, led by a former CEO of a textile export house who wants monthly calls and a seat at the table as an observer.
body.prompt: Which offer is better value, and what would you check before choosing?
body.modelAnswer:
The percentages alone do not settle it. Offer A costs less equity, but the question is what the extra 4% in Offer B buys.
What to check on Offer A: where did the last two cohorts raise their next round, how many actually closed, and are the mentors relevant to a textiles marketplace or mostly consumer app people? Three months in Bengaluru also has a real cost in lost time and attention for a business with paying customers in Jaipur.
What to check on Offer B: is the lead's network genuinely useful, meaning buyers, exporters and logistics partners she cannot reach today? Take references from two founders that lead has already backed, and ask what happened when those companies had a bad quarter. Also confirm the structure: one pooled vehicle on the cap table rather than 25 individual names, and what "observer" means in writing.
A reasonable conclusion: for a niche B2B business with existing revenue, a domain-expert lead who opens buyer doors is usually worth more than a generalist accelerator, so the extra 4% can be good value. Reverse the answer if the accelerator's recent cohorts show a strong record of converting into led seed rounds, which is exactly the evidence she should demand from both sides.

body.title: Diligence the investor, not just the cheque
steps: Ask for two founder references, including at least one company that did not go well.
Check what they actually invest: stage, cheque size, sectors and their last five deals.
Confirm the structure: are you taking one pooled vehicle or many individual names on the cap table?
For a fund or angel fund, confirm the SEBI registration and category.
Ask what they do in a bad quarter, and how they behave when a follow-on round is needed.
Never pay an upfront fee, retainer or success percentage to anyone promising to raise money for you.
Ask how many months of decision time they need, then plan your runway around that answer.

body.title: The gateway registration
body.textWithBlank: To access most central government startup schemes, an eligible Indian startup first needs ___ recognition under Startup India.
body.explanation: Recognition by the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade is free, applied for online, and is the gate to schemes such as the Startup India Seed Fund Scheme and the credit guarantee scheme. Lesson 2.4 covers the eligibility conditions.

cards.definition: An individual investing personal money in early-stage startups, typically ₹2 lakh to ₹25 lakh per company in India.
The investor who diligences a deal, sets terms and invests first, with other investors following into a pooled vehicle.
A pooled angel investment vehicle regulated by SEBI as a sub-category of Category I Alternative Investment Funds.
A small fund, often a few hundred crore, that leads pre-seed and seed rounds with cheques of roughly ₹1 crore to ₹8 crore.
An investor who supplies capital to a VC fund, such as a family office, insurer or government fund-of-funds.
Free government recognition of an eligible startup, and the gateway to most central schemes and tax benefits.
A government programme operated by SIDBI that invests in SEBI-registered AIFs, which in turn invest in startups.

points: Every capital source has a cheque band set by its own structure. Target the ones whose band matches your round.
Individual angels are fastest and most flexible, and operator angels bring introductions and credibility that outlast their money.
Networks, syndicates and platforms pool many small cheques behind one lead, usually landing as a single line on your cap table.
Accelerators sell a package for roughly 5% to 10% equity. Judge them on whether earlier cohorts actually raised a next round.
Fund size dictates cheque size: a ₹3,000 crore fund backing 30 companies has to write around ₹50 crore per first cheque.
Government money through the Startup India Seed Fund Scheme, the Fund of Funds and credit guarantees is slow and milestone linked, but takes no board seat. DPIIT recognition is the gate.
Diligence the investor as hard as they diligence you, and never pay anyone an upfront or success fee to arrange funding.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, legal or financial advice. Investors, funds, accelerators and platforms are named as well-known examples of each category, not as recommendations or endorsements. Cheque sizes are typical market observations, and scheme terms and SEBI thresholds change, so verify current details on official sources before acting. Meher and the Coimbatore and Indore companies are illustrative.
